query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of molybdenum during alloy synthesis, coupled with a subsequent optimized aging treatment, promotes the in‐situ formation of fine, thermally stable Mo-rich precipitates that impede dislocation motion and thereby improve the elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same alloy produced without Mo addition.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy composed of five or more elements (each within 5–35 at%) that is initially produced as a single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 at% molybdenum during melting/fabrication and follow with an optimized post-solidification aging heat treatment.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed under an inert atmosphere and subjected to a controlled aging treatment (e.g., at a temperature between 700°C and 900°C for a designated hold time) and then evaluated under elevated-temperature testing conditions (around 1200°C).
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed, fine Mo-rich precipitates formed within the predominantly Ti/Ni solid-solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening—the formation of fine Mo-rich precipitates impedes dislocation motion and deformation mechanisms during high-temperature service, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-added and aged alloy is expected to exhibit a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the baseline alloy lacking Mo addition and the aging treatment.
generation.baseline: An otherwise identical titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy produced without addition of molybdenum and without the subsequent aging treatment.
generation.boundary: All elemental concentrations must adhere to the HEA definition (5–35 at% each) and the aging parameters must be optimized to promote fine-scale precipitate formation without over-aging or deleterious phase formation; evaluations are carried out at elevated temperatures (≈1200°C).
generation.uncertainty: While the formation of Mo-rich precipitates is expected to enhance strength, the exact improvement magnitude may depend on the precise Mo content, aging parameters, and slight compositional adjustments required to maintain overall phase stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of titanium- and nickel-primary HEA samples: one set with approximately 5 at% Mo addition followed by the prescribed aging heat treatment, and a control set without Mo addition (and consequently without the aging treatment to induce precipitates). Process both sets under identical conditions and perform elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and/or creep tests at ~1200°C) along with microstructural characterization using TEM/SEM.
measurements: Creep resistance (e.g., strain rate or time-to-strain under constant load)
Precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction via microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added and aged alloy does not display a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength or creep resistance compared to the control, or if microstructural analyses do not reveal the expected formation of fine Mo-rich precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory elements, including Rhenium (Re), Molybdenum (Mo), Niobium (Nb), Tantalum (Ta), and Tungsten (W) [] are very important for improving mechanical properties in advanced alloys such as Titanium alloys and Nickel-base superalloys. Generally, elements with a melting point higher than Titanium (Ti), such as Chromium (Cr), Hafnium (Hf), Osmium (Os), Ruthenium (Ru), Vanadium (V), and Zirconium (Zr) are also classified as refractory elements. In Titanium alloys, refractory elements, especially Mo and W, are all beta stabilizers and possess a strong solid solution strengthening characteristic []. Nb forms Ni3Nb γ phase in Nickel-base superalloys such as Inconel 718 []. The improved creep resistance of the sixth generation superalloy TMS-238 mainly results from Re and Ru additions []. Refractory alloys also play significant roles in industry. In the second generation nuclear power plants, the most-used materials for fuel cladding are Zircoloy 2 and Zircoloy 4. The Niobium alloy C103 is used for the nozzle extension of satellites []. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as alloys that are composed of more than 4 elements with near equi-atomic percentage [,,,]. Due to their high mixing entropy, HEAs tend to form simple solid-solution phases, such as face-centered-cubic (FCC) [,], body-centered-cubic (BCC) [,,], and hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) structures [,]. With the entropic stabilization of solid-solution phases, HEAs have attracted significant attention, because of their outstanding properties at elevated temperatures, which results from severe lattice distortion and microstructural stability at high temperatures [,,]. Many refractory HEAs (RHEAs), which mainly consist of BCC-type single solid-solution phase, have been developed and investigated due to their excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures []. The excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures in RHEAs are significantly associated with their unique atomic structures (distorted lattices) and high melting temperatures of the constitutive refractory elements (Ti, Nb, V, Mo, Ta, W, and Cr) [,,,]. The aim of the current work was to develop and design new RHEAs, which have low density and high strength at elevated temperature for high-temperature applications. The density of the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) alloys was measured to be approximately 5.84 g cm−3, which is slightly larger density than the Al0.8NbTiV alloy (5.61 g cm−3) due to the addition of Co and Ni. However, this value is much lower than conventional high-temperature materials, such as Inconel 718 (8.22 g cm−3) [] and RHEAs. Most reported RHEAs possess high density of 6–13 g cm−3, i.e., NbTiVZr and CrNbTiVZr alloys are 6.52 and 6.57 g cm−3 [], respectively. drafts.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of zirconium (≈5 at%) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature mechanical properties by promoting the in situ formation of fine, stable Zr-containing precipitates that inhibit dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents (along with at least three other elements in the 5–35 at% range) having a predominantly homogeneous single‐phase solid solution.
drafts.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 at% zirconium into the alloy during synthesis.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is synthesized using arc melting followed by homogenization and a controlled heat-treatment process to encourage precipitate formation, with mechanical tests conducted at high temperatures (e.g., between 600°C and 800°C).
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a dispersion of fine, Zr-containing precipitates within the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: Zirconium segregates during the heat-treatment to form stable intermetallic precipitates, which act as obstacles to dislocation movement and grain-boundary sliding. This dispersion strengthening hinders high-temperature creep and enhances yield strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The zirconium-modified alloy will show improved elevated-temperature creep resistance and yield strength relative to the baseline alloy without zirconium.
drafts.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy synthesized and processed under identical conditions but without the addition of zirconium.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is limited to approximately 5 at% zirconium addition; performance improvements are expected under high-temperature operating conditions between 600°C and 800°C. The overall alloy composition must still adhere to the high-entropy alloy definition (five or more elements at 5–35 at% each).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloys with identical base compositions: one set with an added 5 at% zirconium and one set without (control). Process both sets via arc melting, homogenization, and identical heat-treatment schedules designed to promote precipitate formation. Perform mechanical tests (creep tests and yield strength measurements) at 600°C, 700°C, and 800°C. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to characterize the presence, distribution, and morphology of precipitates.
measurements: Creep strain rates at elevated temperatures
Yield strength values at selected high temperatures
Precipitate volume fraction and distribution from microstructural analysis (TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the zirconium-added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., >10%) improvement in creep resistance or yield strength over the control samples, and if TEM analysis does not show a notable increase in fine, well-dispersed Zr-containing precipitates compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding approximately 5 at% tungsten to a titanium–nickel–primary high-entropy alloy will lead to the in situ formation of fine, tungsten-rich precipitates during processing and subsequent heat treatment, which will impede dislocation motion and improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without tungsten.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are primary constituents (each roughly 30–45 at%) along with three or more additional elements (each within 5–35 at%) that together meet the compositional criteria.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate ~5 at% tungsten into the alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is processed (e.g., cast and homogenized) and subjected to a post-solidification heat treatment at an elevated temperature (e.g., 700°C) that promotes precipitation during service conditions typical of high-temperature applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of fine-scale, tungsten-rich precipitates dispersed within the disordered matrix.
drafts.mechanism: W-rich precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and help to stabilize the microstructure at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength, creep resistance, and overall high-temperature performance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-alloyed sample is predicted to exhibit improved mechanical performance at elevated temperatures (e.g., increased yield strength and reduced creep rate) compared to a compositionally identical alloy lacking tungsten.
drafts.baseline: An otherwise identical titanium–nickel–primary high-entropy alloy without the added tungsten.
drafts.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within the compositional range (each element between 5–35 at%), under elevated service temperatures around 600–800°C, and given a heat treatment schedule that allows for controlled precipitation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys with identical base compositions: one set with ~5 at% tungsten and one without tungsten. Subject both sets to identical processing and heat treatment conditions designed to promote precipitation. Test both sets at an elevated temperature (e.g., 700°C) under constant load to assess high-temperature mechanical performance.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to verify the presence and distribution of tungsten-rich precipitates in the tungsten-alloyed samples.
Mechanical testing such as high-temperature tensile tests and constant-load creep tests to measure yield strength and creep rates.
Comparative analysis of the mechanical properties between tungsten-containing and tungsten-free alloys.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the tungsten-added alloy does not demonstrably exhibit statistically significant improvements in yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperature, or if microstructural analysis fails to show a distinct formation of fine tungsten-rich precipitates compared to the tungsten-free baseline under the specified processing conditions.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of molybdenum (Mo) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of fine, thermally stable Mo-rich precipitates during proper heat treatment, thereby enhancing the alloy’s elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the same material without Mo.
drafts.material_initial_state: A five-element high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents (e.g., approximately 30 at% Ti and 30 at% Ni) along with three secondary elements chosen to maintain the HEA definition (each between 5–35 at%), and initially present as a single-phase solid solution.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate approximately 15 at% molybdenum into the alloy formulation (by adjusting the content of one or more of the minor elements) and apply a controlled heat-treatment schedule designed to induce the formation of fine Mo-rich precipitates.
drafts.conditions: The alloy should be processed and tested under elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., in the range of 1200–1600°C) with identical thermal histories for both the baseline and Mo-added compositions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The emergence of uniformly distributed, fine Mo-rich precipitates (for example, a sigma phase) within the solid-solution matrix.
drafts.mechanism: Molybdenum, due to its high melting point and strong atomic interactions, increases the overall thermal stability and promotes the precipitation of Mo-rich phases during heat treatment. These precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion at high temperatures, thereby improving yield strength and creep resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Mo-added alloy is expected to show a statistically significant increase (e.g., on the order of ≥10% higher yield strength) at elevated temperatures, along with improved creep performance, compared to the baseline titanium-nickel primary alloy.
drafts.baseline: A titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy of similar overall composition that does not contain the additional molybdenum intended to form strengthening precipitates.
drafts.boundary: Alloy compositions must adhere to the HEA definition (each principal element between 5–35 at%) and the improved properties are targeted for operation in environments up to approximately 1600°C.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two samples of the titanium- and nickel-primary HEA: one as the baseline and one with an added 15 at% Mo (with corresponding adjustments in the remaining minor elements), ensuring both batches are processed (melted, cast, and heat-treated) under identical conditions. Subject both sample sets to elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compressive tests at 1200°C) and perform microstructural analysis to quantify the size and distribution of any precipitates formed.
measurements: Precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution (via TEM or SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added alloy does not display a statistically significant increase (on the order of at least 10%) in yield strength or creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline alloy, or if no distinct fine Mo-rich precipitates are observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy (HEA), the deliberate addition of ~5 at% molybdenum followed by an optimized aging heat treatment will promote the precipitation of fine, stable Ti–Mo/Ni–Mo intermetallic phases that act as nanoscale obstacles to dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance compared to the same alloy without Mo addition and aging.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy composed primarily of titanium and nickel along with three other refractory elements (for example, Nb, V, and Cr) where each element is present between 5 and 35 atomic percent, ensuring a uniform solid-solution state.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate approximately 5 atomic percent molybdenum into the alloy composition during melting, then apply a post-solidification aging heat treatment (e.g., hold at 700–900 °C for about 2 hours) to trigger controlled precipitation.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is processed under an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, and its mechanical properties are evaluated under elevated-temperature conditions (around 1200 °C). The aging treatment must be precisely controlled to avoid over-aging or precipitate coarsening.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation and uniform dispersion of fine, nanoscale intermetallic precipitates (e.g., Ti–Mo and/or Ni–Mo phases) within the predominantly Ti/Ni solid-solution matrix.
drafts.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: the fine intermetallic precipitates hinder dislocation glide and creep deformation during high-temperature exposure, thereby increasing yield strength and improving resistance to creep.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Mo-added and aged alloy will display a statistically significant increase in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance (e.g., higher stress retention at or near 1200 °C) relative to the baseline alloy lacking Mo addition and without aging-induced precipitates.
drafts.baseline: The same Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy produced without the molybdenum addition and without the post-solidification aging step.
drafts.boundary: All elemental concentrations must remain within the 5–35 at% range to satisfy the HEA compositional definition; the aging parameters (temperature and duration) must be optimized to promote fine-scale precipitate formation without triggering excessive coarsening or forming deleterious phases.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the Ti–Ni primary HEA: one batch with ~5 at% Mo addition and subsequent aging heat treatment at 700–900 °C for 2 hours, and a control batch without Mo addition (or without the aging treatment). Process both batches under identical conditions and measure their high-temperature mechanical performance.
measurements: Creep resistance (e.g., time to a defined strain under constant load at high temperature)
Microstructural analysis via TEM/SEM to confirm the presence, size, and distribution of precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added and aged alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and/or creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the control alloy, or if no fine precipitates are observed via microstructural analysis, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
